title_en: Hong Kong flight makes emergency landing in Philippines after engine fire alert
content_en:
Air Niugini flight PX19 to Port Moresby in Papua New Guinea landed safely with 146 passengers and crew on board.
The aircraft made an emergency landing at Davao International Airport. Photo: X/arunruby08
A flight from Hong Kong to Papua New Guinea carrying 146 passengers and crew made an emergency landing in the southern Philippines early on Saturday over a potential engine fire.
Air Niugini’s flight PX19 to Port Moresby, the capital of Papua New Guinea, made the unscheduled stop at Davao International Airport at about 12.08am, according to Philippine media, citing the Civil Aviation Authority of the Philippines (CAAP).
The Boeing 767-300 landed safely, and the 137 passengers and nine crew members disembarked through emergency slides. No injuries were reported.
The pilots reportedly received an indication of possible sparks or a fire involving the aircraft’s right engine, prompting them to divert.
A subsequent assessment disclosed damage to all four right-side landing gear wheels.
The airport was temporarily closed for the emergency response and safety checks before reopening at 2.05am.
A CAAP aircraft accident investigator was sent to the scene.
By Fiona Sun

title_en: Weak yen, tax cuts put Japan’s defence plans in a Trump bind
content_en:
Scaled-back spending targets have infuriated conservatives and could put Tokyo on a collision course with the White House.
Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi gestures as US President Donald Trump speaks during their visit to the aircraft carrier USS George Washington at the US Navy’s Yokosuka base, south of Tokyo, in October 2025. Photo: AP
Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi is facing growing backlash from fellow conservatives over plans to rein in the country’s next five-year defence budget, but analysts say pressure from Washington could pose an even bigger challenge.
The dispute pits demands for a stronger military against Japan’s economic constraints, with a weak yen and concerns over government finances complicating Takaichi’s efforts to satisfy both her political allies and US President Donald Trump.
The Finance Ministry has indicated that it is prepared to allocate between 50 trillion yen and 60 trillion yen (US$314 billion to US$377 billion) over five years from April 2027, well short of the 80 trillion yen advocated by some members of the ruling Liberal Democratic Party, military planners and the US, which is pushing its allies to spend at least 3.5 per cent of gross domestic product on defence.
That figure would still be a significant increase on the current 43 trillion yen five-year plan, which had been scheduled to run until March 2028, but conservatives say it falls short of what is needed to protect the nation amid deepening regional security concerns and growing pressure from Washington for Tokyo to fund more of its own defence.
“If the figure comes to 55 trillion yen over five years, calculations that take into account inflation and the yen’s exchange rate show this would amount to 1.7 per cent of GDP,” said Tsutomu Nishioka, a visiting professor at Reitaku University and a senior member of the conservative Japan Institute for National Fundamentals (JINF) think tank.
“It does not even reach 2 per cent and would constitute a breach of our international commitments,” he said.
With the government due to approve revisions to the three documents that guide national security planning in the coming weeks, another JINF official accused Tokyo of “effectively undermining efforts to strengthen Japan’s defence capabilities”.
In a paper published by the think tank, JINF vice-president Kiyofumi Iwata pointed out that even with the increase being offered by the Finance Ministry, the cost of defence equipment and components imported from the US has risen dramatically because of the weaker yen, while fuel purchases are also priced in dollars.
Japanese, US and Australian F-35 stealth fighters fly in formation during Exercise Cope North over the Indo-Pacific in February 2025. Photo: US Air Force
Iwata also cited what he described as a growing threat from Beijing, arguing that its “preparations for an invasion of Taiwan are making steady progress, as evidenced by its military build-up and large-scale exercises by the People’s Liberation Army”, while pointing to naval drills in the western Pacific.
Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the US, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-governed island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons.
“Under these circumstances, one cannot help but doubt whether the Sanae Takaichi administration, which is moving towards an effective reduction in defence spending, is seriously committed to the survival of the nation and the safety of its people,” said Iwata, a former chief of staff of Japan’s Ground Self-Defence Force.
Echoing the position of LDP members and other conservatives, Iwata suggested issuing government bonds to cover defence spending, adding: “Is it not the role of politicians to demonstrate an even greater determination in Japan, which faces multiple threats from neighbouring countries?”
Yoichi Shimada, a professor emeritus at Fukui Prefectural University and former lawmaker with Japan’s Conservative Party, said the nation faced broad financial challenges, particularly given that Takaichi has committed her administration to temporarily reducing the consumption tax on food at a time of growing economic discomfort for many Japanese.
“An increase in defence spending is inevitable and although I am rarely happy with the Ministry of Finance because all it seems to want to do is raise taxes, I do understand the issues here,” he said.
“I believe the government needs to be much cleverer in the way it spends the defence budget,” Shimada added, pointing to the drone warfare as an evolution Japan’s armed forces could replicate.
While Shimada said the rumblings of discontent within the party were undeniable, he added that the issue did not threaten Takaichi’s leadership because of the large majority that her coalition enjoyed.
“Most members of the party are still very strongly behind Takaichi,” he said, referring to the LDP.
“This is a point of contention, and she will have heard their voices, but I do not see it becoming a major problem for her as leader>”
With the revised defence budget falling far short of what Washington is demanding of its allies, Go Ito, a professor of politics and international relations at Tokyo’s Meiji University, said he believed Trump might be of greater concern to Takaichi.
“Successive prime ministers have been gradually increasing the defence budget, but Takaichi made it clear from the outset that she planned to make a very sharp increase in spending, in part because that was what the US was demanding,” he said.
The Japanese government was acutely aware of the importance of the military alliance with the US, Ito said, and Takaichi had signalled that Japan was a reliable partner and would meet Trump’s demands.
Economic realities over the past 18 months, most notably the decline of the yen, had made that position far harder to maintain, he added.
A US military aircraft takes off from Kadena Air Base in Okinawa, Japan, in 2023. Photo: Reuters
Washington also has control over a powerful pressure point, in the form of thousands of US military personnel stationed at bases across Japan.
National broadcaster NHK reported on Sunday that Trump’s administration had instructed Japan to pay more than 3 trillion yen over five years from April 2027 to host US forces in the country. That figure is nearly three times what Japan currently pays, with negotiations reportedly ongoing.
“Different factions within the LDP have different positions on greater defence spending, but I think Takaichi’s biggest problem is going to be dealing with the US,” Ito said.
By Julian Ryall

title_en: Australia-Philippine deal exposes where Asean’s architecture is weakest
content_en:
As bilateral and minilateral deals grow more common, Asean risks retaining the language of centrality while losing influence over the substance of regional security.
Australia’s Prime Minister Anthony Albanese (left) walks with Philippine Secretary of National Defence Gilberto Teodoro Jnr ahead of the signing ceremony for the Philippines-Australia Defense Cooperation Arrangement in Manila on November 15. Photo: Reuters
The most revealing moment of the 49th Asean summit in Manila might have occurred beyond the plenary hall. On November 15, as Southeast Asian governments gathered to reaffirm regional cooperation, Australia and the Philippines signed a new defence cooperation arrangement intended to make their military partnership more practical.
The timing was striking: the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) was celebrating its central role even as two partners were building security mechanisms outside its institutional framework. This is not a mutual defence treaty between Australia and the Philippines, but it gives their partnership greater strategic depth.
The move sits within a wider pattern. On October 28, defence ministers from Australia, Japan, the Philippines and the United States met in Cebu on the sidelines of the Asean Defence Ministers’ Meeting-Plus. They agreed to establish a combined coordination centre in the Philippines, coordinate defence investment and expand joint exercises.
Neither Canberra nor Manila intends to abandon Asean. Their Kasandigan statement explicitly reaffirmed Asean centrality and the Asean-led regional architecture. That is precisely what makes the development significant: governments can endorse Asean’s diplomatic leadership while relying on smaller partnerships to deliver capabilities that regional institutions do not provide. The question is whether Asean centrality extends beyond convening meetings and articulating principles to shaping the practical priorities and capabilities of regional security.
Asean centrality has long rested on its ability to convene major powers, sustain dialogue and provide an inclusive diplomatic framework. Through the Asean Regional Forum, the East Asia Summit and the Asean Defence Ministers’ Meeting-Plus, it has brought countries with competing interests into the same institutional space. Its value lies not in commanding armies but in preventing the strongest powers from dictating regional order.
However, convening power is not the same as strategic agency. Asean has no collective defence obligation, standing military command or integrated force structure. Its consensus-based decision-making protects the equality of members, but it also makes common responses difficult when threat perceptions diverge.
Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese (left) and Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jnr show documents on defence agreements during a bilateral meeting on the sidelines of the 49th Asean Summit in Manila on November 16. Photo: AFP
The demand for more focused cooperation is therefore understandable. Lowy Institute research published in 2025 found that Australia, India and Japan collectively concluded 38 new defence agreements with Southeast Asian countries between 2017 and 2024, compared with 22 by the US and China combined. More than 80 per cent of 51 new defence dialogue mechanisms established since 2017 involved maritime Southeast Asia and Vietnam. These figures point to a geography of security engagement increasingly shaped by states most exposed to maritime competition.
Australia’s role deserves particular attention. It is not simply an auxiliary to Washington’s regional strategy. Canberra has its own interests in secure sea lanes, stable supply chains and a predictable maritime order. Its expanding defence relationship with Manila deepens Australia’s defence coordination with a strategically positioned partner while helping the Philippines develop surveillance, logistics and operational capabilities. For Manila, the arrangement diversifies external support without requiring it to place every security need within a single alliance.
The wider environment adds urgency. The Stockholm International Peace Research Institute estimates military spending in Asia and Oceania reached US$681 billion in 2025, an 8.1 per cent real increase. China’s spending rose 7.4 per cent to US$336 billion, while Japan’s reached US$62.2 billion.
Meanwhile, the ISEAS-Yusof Ishak Institute’s latest State of Southeast Asia survey found 51.7 per cent of regional respondents were concerned about encroachments into Southeast Asian coastal states’ exclusive economic zones and continental shelves while 45.2 per cent feared an accidental clash between an Asean member and China. The figures do not prove minilateralism is the answer but help explain the demand for faster, specialised cooperation.
[embedded media]
The danger for Asean is not that Australia and the Philippines are cooperating more closely. Their partnership can contribute to maritime stability, disaster response and deterrence. The deeper risk is that operational standards, information-sharing and crisis coordination develop through exclusive arrangements beyond Asean’s influence. If that happens, Asean could retain the language of centrality while losing influence over the substance of regional security.
Bilateral and minilateral exercises need not be absorbed into Asean, but their lessons and standards can be shared. Indonesia has a particular stake in this effort. Its geography around the Natuna waters and the Malacca, Sunda and Lombok straits makes maritime stability a direct national concern. Jakarta has defence relationships of its own, but it must ensure these partnerships strengthen both national readiness and regional confidence. Indonesia can combine better maritime surveillance with efforts to make Asean-led mechanisms more useful in preventing incidents and managing crises.
Asean does not need to monopolise regional security cooperation to remain central. It must, however, retain a meaningful role in setting the agenda, shaping norms and connecting the networks that are emerging around it. Australia and the Philippines are not dismantling Asean’s architecture; they are exposing where it is weakest. The test of Asean centrality will be whether the organisation can influence what happens beyond its meeting rooms.
By Ronny P. Sasmita

title_en: Hong Kong’s tourism edge lies in the East-meets-West experience
content_en:
Halloween celebrations, The Weeknd concert and the Wine and Dine Festival showed that simultaneous major events can attract both mainland and overseas interest.
Visitors enjoy the festive decor at Statue Square in Central on November 18 when Hong Kong kicked off its Winterfest events. Photo: Karma Lo
Halloween and the Christmas festive season may be dissimilar events, but similar tourism formulas could work for them both. While Hong Kong has long been known as a place where East meets West, Halloween has just dramatised its untapped unique tourism potential.
The city’s first Halloween month – as opposed to a one-day event – proved a hit with locals and visitors alike. It has set the scene for an expanded version of the annual Winterfest, from November 18 to January 5, embracing Christmas and New Year.
Halloween month culminated in extraordinary scenes on the big night as costumed revellers packed the Lan Kwai Fong entertainment area and bars saw a big boost to business. It has now joined Hong Kong’s busy mega-events programme, an integral part of tourism’s key role in the country’s 15th five-year plan and the city’s first five-year plan.
What also set the month apart was the concurrence, in the final week of Halloween, of a sell-out series of concerts by Canadian entertainer The Weeknd at the 50,000-seat Kai Tak stadium, and the city’s annual Wine and Dine Festival at the Central harbourfront events space. As a result, mainland visitors for the concerts may also have visited a Halloween event and perhaps even the Wine and Dine Festival.
Travellers from the mainland and from as far away as London described the Halloween celebration as a “must-see”, despite the long waits to enter some streets. The Halloween programme, which began on October 17, involved street celebrations in Central including Lan Kwai Fong, Kai Tak, Mong Kok and Tsim Sha Tsui East on three consecutive Saturdays, culminating on Halloween night.
Simultaneous major events can prompt tourist interest not just on the mainland but overseas, and could be a good way of encouraging visitors to extend overnight stays.
Since the East-meets-West aspect of events like Halloween appears to appeal to mainlanders, it seems to be the way to go in promoting the festive tourist season. Accordingly, the tourism authorities have adopted a decentralised approach to Winterfest. It will expand beyond Central this year with new attractions including steam trains and aurora light shows.
This year’s Winterfest will feature a winter wonderland at Statue Square Gardens in Central, which will have a 22-metre-tall outdoor Christmas tree, two metres taller than last year’s.
The Central winter wonderland will also include festive installations such as a 12-metre-long steam train, prancing reindeer and vintage toy hot-air balloons, alongside Christmas markets and a mailing corner where visitors can shop and send seasonal wishes to loved ones.
Nine buildings in Central will serve as the canvas for an immersive, train-themed light show spanning eight acts. It will run every 30 minutes from 7pm to 11pm.
This is the first time the festival will expand to the major commercial districts of Tsim Sha Tsui and Causeway Bay, with the latter programme to run slightly later from November 25 to January 3.
“These highlights will encourage more locals and visitors to stay and spend in Hong Kong, immerse themselves in the city’s unique winter experiences, and discover the festive charm found only in Hong Kong,” Tourism Board chairman Peter Lam Kin-ngok said.
But the festival’s opening also marked the final performance of “A Symphony of Lights”, the nightly Victoria Harbour show that has illuminated the city’s skyline for 22 years. It will be replaced by seasonal light shows. The final performance included special rooftop pyrotechnic effects and fireworks launched along the shores of Victoria Harbour.
“A Symphony of Lights” has illuminated Victoria Harbour since 2004. Last month, authorities also scrapped a controversial plan to install decorative lights along a scenic trail on The Peak, which was intended to boost the city’s nighttime tourism appeal. The decision followed public outcry over the removal of trees and vegetation, as well as light pollution.
That said, the East-meets-West experience gives Hong Kong a genuine edge in the international tourist market. It will need to be constantly sharpened if we are to remain competitive.
By SCMP Editorial

title_en: Xi’s Apec summit speech is a call to cooperation suited to the times
content_en:
An ancient Chinese saying Xi has quoted on several occasions highlights the paradox of an increasingly interconnected yet highly competitive world.
Illustration: Mario Rivera
In his keynote speech at the Apec CEO Summit in Shenzhen on November 18, President Xi Jinping quoted the ancient Chinese saying “fan yi zhi dao yu shi jie xing”, which suggests that all approaches must move with the times to be of benefit.
Of all the messages in his speech, the eight characters of the Chinese saying caught my attention. Rooted in the I Ching, or Book of Changes, the phrase carries a simple but important idea: progress comes from creating benefits while recognising that the ways to achieve them must change with the times.
It speaks to a paradox of our age. The world has never been more interconnected. Economies, technologies and supply chains depend on one another more than ever but some countries still seek to build barriers and retreat into competing blocs.
Perhaps the answer to this paradox lies just in those eight characters. What makes the phrase particularly interesting is that Xi has used it on several occasions in the past decade, in speeches addressing different international issues. Its repeated appearance suggests it is more than a literary reference – it offers a consistent way of thinking about how countries should respond to a changing world.
In June 2014, at a gathering marking the 60th anniversary of the Five Principles of Peaceful Coexistence, Xi invoked the saying while discussing how these principles could remain relevant in a changing international environment. The message was that long-standing principles should not become outdated simply because the world around them changes. Instead, they need to be upheld and put into practice in new circumstances.
In October 2015, during a speech at Guildhall in London’s financial district, he used the same phrase in the context of China-UK relations and global economic cooperation. The focus was on seizing opportunities and opening a new chapter in bilateral relations. The underlying idea was that countries could create more opportunities for themselves by working together rather than turning away from one another.
Chinese President Xi Jinping signs the distinguished visitors book watched by the then lord mayor of London Alan Yarrow, before a banquet at the Guildhall, in London on October 21, 2015. Photo: AP
The following months brought another application of this thinking. At the opening ceremony of the second World Internet Conference in December 2015, the phrase appeared in the context of international cooperation in cyberspace. As digital technology transforms economies and societies, countries need to develop new approaches to cooperation and governance.
The issues were different, from international relations and economic ties to digital governance, but the central idea remained relevant. Principles can endure, but the ways of applying them need to evolve.
This distinction matters today. Adapting to change is often mistaken for giving in to it. However, moving with the times does not mean following every trend or abandoning one’s principles. It means understanding new realities and finding practical ways to respond without losing sight of the goals that matter.
Consider the debate over economic security. Many governments want to make their supply chains more resilient and reduce strategic risks. These are legitimate concerns, but resilience should not become a synonym for isolation. Diversifying trade and investment links can make economies stronger. Cutting off cooperation altogether makes them more vulnerable.
[embedded media]
The same question applies to technology. Artificial intelligence (AI) is changing industries, creating new markets and raising difficult questions about safety, access and governance. While competition will remain part of this process, countries also have shared interests in setting rules, managing risks and ensuring technological progress benefits more than just a handful of economies and companies.
This is where the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) framework matters. The Asia-Pacific’s economic success is built in large part on trade, investment and connected production networks. Economies at different stages of development have found ways to participate in regional growth. Differences among them still exist, but they have created shared interests that give cooperation a practical foundation.
Apec needs to adapt its agenda to new realities while preserving the principle that made regional cooperation valuable in the first place. Xi’s speech pointed to several areas where this effort could take shape: maintaining open trade and investment, keeping supply chains stable, deepening cooperation in digital technology and AI, and promoting greener and more inclusive growth. These matters go beyond governments and influence where businesses invest, how people earn a living and what households can afford.
There is also a broader question of who benefits from growth. Technological progress and regional integration will have limited value if their gains remain concentrated in a few economies or sectors. Developing economies and small businesses need opportunities to participate. Cooperation must deliver tangible benefits if it is to retain public support.
[embedded media]
This is an important part of the meaning of “fan yi zhi dao yu shi xie xing”. The pursuit of benefit should not be understood as a race in which one side gains only at another’s expense. In an interconnected world, lasting progress depends on recognising shared interests and expanding the benefits available to all.
No ancient saying can resolve today’s geopolitical tensions or remove the differences between nations. Neither does adapting to the times mean countries must agree on everything. However, it can offer a useful starting point: change is inevitable, but isolation is a choice.
The world needs to find a form of cooperation suited to today’s realities. For the Asia-Pacific, that means keeping markets open, making supply chains more resilient, sharing the opportunities created by new technologies and ensuring growth reaches more people. The real test of leadership is how well countries can work with each other to adapt the changing world.
More than a decade after Xi first invoked the phrase in an international setting, its relevance has not diminished. The challenges have changed, but the need to adapt while creating shared benefits remains.

title_en: Icebreaker: China-led global standard could boost its shipbuilding clout, Arctic share
content_en:
The standard tests how much resistance ships face when breaking through snow-covered ice and ice loads on offshore oil, gas platforms.
A China-led framework will set global safety standards for ships in polar waters after the Zhong Shan Da Xue Ji Di successfully completed a sea trial in the ice area of ​​the Bohai Sea. Photo: SYSU
A new China-led international standard for testing ships and offshore structures in snow-covered ice could further strengthen its shipbuilding industry and help it capture a larger share of the growing polar shipping market, an industry analyst said.
Recently published by the International Organisation for Standardisation, it sets out a common framework for model tests that estimate how much resistance ships face when breaking through snow-covered ice, as well as the ice loads on offshore structures. Both are critical to safe operations in polar waters.
Offshore structures usually refer to human-made facilities built at sea, such as oil and gas platforms and offshore wind turbines.
Led by China and developed with experts from the United States, South Korea, Japan, Britain and Iran, among other countries, the standard “provides important technical support for improving the safety of polar shipping and refining the design of polar marine engineering equipment”, state broadcaster CCTV reported on Monday.
Chen Fei’er, a lecturer at Shanghai Jiao Tong University’s School of Ocean and Civil Engineering, said its publication also carried “political significance” amid Beijing’s push for technological self-reliance.
China, she said, had traditionally been “more of a technology follower”, making it difficult for the country to lead the drafting of standards for established products and equipment.
But emerging fields such as polar shipping had opened an opportunity to shape global standards, incentivised in part by its strength in shipbuilding, she added.
China leads the global shipbuilding industry in terms of new orders, though it is still working to close the technological gap with South Korea in high-value segments such as liquefied natural gas carriers.
[embedded media]
The standard’s release comes amid growing interest in Arctic shipping, both to bypass geopolitical risks on traditional maritime routes to Europe and to access the region’s vast energy resources. That interest is fuelling demand for vessels and offshore equipment built to operate in extreme conditions.
However, engineers had long struggled to assess the forces snow-covered ice can exert on ships and offshore structures. Without a common international testing standard, results from different countries were difficult to compare, making it hard to judge how reliable the tests were, according to the CCTV report.
Snow changes the surface of sea ice and how it breaks apart, affecting the resistance ships face when breaking through ice, the report said.
Despite an increase in voyages by Chinese and South Korean operators through Arctic waters to Europe this year, unpredictable ice conditions remained one of the key challenges facing operators and have contributed to delays, according to a recent report by the Oslo-based Bellona Foundation.
Commercially, the standard could create new opportunities for China’s shipbuilding industry, according to Chen.
Vessels operating in the region require specialised support, including icebreakers to clear paths through frozen waters, while commercial ships need hull structures and steel capable of withstanding different conditions from those encountered in conventional shipping routes, she said.
“If China can make breakthroughs in the relevant technologies, other countries may also want [these vessels], creating opportunities for Chinese manufacturers to supply more ships capable of navigating Arctic routes,” she added.
By Sherry Wang

title_en: Recovery at last? Analysts divided on China’s home market outlook
content_en:
As local governments face land-sale revenue shortfalls, the question of when the sector will truly bottom out sparks debate.
Workers construct a new residential complex in Hangzhou, in eastern China’s Zhejiang province, on October 19. Photo: VCG via Getty Images
How long the property slump in mainland China will continue remains an ominous question for the world’s second-largest economy, where local governments’ fiscal revenue largely hinges on land sales.
While economists agree that falling home prices – the “enemy within” for the economy – continue to wreak havoc on consumer spending, employment, fixed-asset investment and business confidence, they are still divided on when the property sector will truly hit bottom.
The slumbering home market continued to hugely dent developers’ land-buying interest, making it a serious problem for local economies, as regional authorities lacked financial powder to fuel retail sales and bolster infrastructure construction, said Song Yu, chief China economist at UBS Securities.
“Real estate policies can be implemented in a more flexible manner to allow for some room for local governments to manoeuvre,” he said. “More drastic easing measures can be introduced, such as further reducing homebuyers’ down payment ratios and another cut in mortgage rates.”
The property crisis began in 2021 after Beijing rolled out austerity measures to deleverage an industry facing mounting financial risks, which led to developer defaults and spiralling confidence that dragged home prices down by more than 22 per cent over the past six years, according to S&P Global Ratings.
The rating agency estimated in a research report last month that housing prices on the mainland could bottom out in the third quarter of 2028, when a sharp drop in new home supply was set to trigger a favourable change in the supply-demand balance.
“Tier-one cities will likely recover sooner, in 2027, driven by more resilient homebuying demand in these large cities,” S&P added.
China’s real estate sector and related industries, such as home appliances and construction materials, accounted for about a quarter of economic output, according to analysts.
For local governments, proceeds from land auctions made up as much as 40 per cent of fiscal income before 2021, when 8.7 trillion yuan (US$1.3 trillion) worth of land parcels were sold across the mainland.
In the first three quarters of 2026, land sales brought in 1.61 trillion yuan, a 27.9 per cent drop from a year earlier.
A recovery of the property market in 2028 seems to be a very optimistic forecastYou Liangzhou, Shanghai property agency owner
A buoyant property market would not only spur construction, create jobs and boost local government’s coffers but also expand personal wealth for homeowners, encouraging them to increase their spending on daily necessities, said Yu Xiangrong, Citigroup’s chief economist for Greater China.
But Yu did not expect that to happen soon. He predicted early this month that total proceeds from land sales across the mainland would further decline by 1 trillion yuan in 2027.
“A recovery of the property market in 2028 seems to be a very optimistic forecast,” said You Liangzhou, the owner of the Baonuo property agency in Shanghai. “Despite stable [home] prices being seen in Shanghai, most of our clients remain cautious about the outlook because they still believe the local home market is frothy.”
China’s residential property market took off in the early 1990s amid the country’s economic reform and measures to open its economy up to the world.
Prices of flats in Shanghai’s downtown areas surged more than 20-fold before 2020, buoyed by breakneck economic growth and increasing housing demand.
The “three red lines” clampdown, initiated in August 2020, however, marked a watershed for the Chinese property sector.
The framework capped debt-to-asset ratios for developers at 70 per cent after excluding advance receipts, limited net debt-to-equity ratios to 100 per cent and held short-term borrowing to no more than cash reserves.
Government incentives are not strong enough to restore our confidenceYu Xiaosen, Shanghai graduate
The stringent requirements forced more than 50 mainland developers to default on some US$100 billion worth of offshore bonds between 2021 and 2022, according to a JPMorgan report.
Positive sentiment remains in short supply among potential buyers, despite the years of price reductions.
“We still feel it difficult for us to buy a flat given the current prices, even after a nearly 30 per cent drop from the peak,” said Yu Xiaosen, a fresh university graduate in Shanghai. “Government incentives are not strong enough to restore our confidence.”
In August, Beijing extended mortgage terms to facilitate homebuying for middle- and low-income consumers.
A month later, the central government also announced that a mortgage interest subsidy policy for first-time homebuyers would come into effect from October 1.
But the policies have failed to stop a downward spiral in home transactions and prices in mainland China’s lower-tier cities.
By Daniel Ren

title_en: ‘Horrific’ ICE arrests at Seattle airport jet bridge rattle passengers, fuel outrage
content_en:
The incident caused a ‘distressing’ scene for Alaska Airlines passengers and delayed the Los Angeles-bound flight.
Travellers walk by an Alaska Airlines bag drop area at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport on Monday. Photo: AP
Masked immigration officers detained two people on a crowded airport jet bridge in Seattle as people were boarding on Saturday, causing what Alaska Airlines called a “distressing” scene for passengers and employees and delaying the Los Angeles-bound flight.
Video of the incident showed officers dragging away at least one person at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport as a woman screams that her daughter is being taken and she has a work permit.
Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) said in a statement that its officers conducted a targeted enforcement operation to arrest Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza, an immigrant from Mexico who “overstayed his visa in violation of our nation’s laws”.
During the confrontation, another passenger “hurled hot coffee on the officers”, the ICE statement said. That woman, Sofia Hernandez Mejia, was determined to be in the United States illegally from Mexico and to have also overstayed her visa, ICE said. She could be charged with assaulting a federal officer.
Online flight data showed that Alaska flight 1306, which had been scheduled to depart at 8.10am (local time), was delayed.
Alaska Airlines said ICE officers gave no advance notice of the enforcement action, which occurred during a busy travel weekend ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday.
“We are concerned by this morning’s law enforcement action during the boarding of Alaska flight 1306,” the airline said. “We recognise how distressing this incident has been for affected employees and guests.”
It added that the airline is committed to “treating every guest with dignity and respect”.
The arresting officers wore unmarked jackets and khaki trousers. The video showed them struggling with someone on the ground as passengers surrounded by rolling suitcases looked on.
[embedded media]
ICE has stepped up arrests at airports since the summer, especially targeting people who overstayed visas in the past.
Alaska Airlines said it was working with the Port of Seattle, which manages the airport, to see if protocols were followed, and also that it has raised concerns “directly with the appropriate authorities”.
The Port of Seattle said in a statement that the arrest was distressing not only for the affected family but for other passengers, and that local authorities would “engage federal officials to understand more about what occurred”.
Washington Governor Bob Ferguson, a Democrat, said ICE’s tactics were “deeply un-American” and called for the agency’s abolition.

title_en: Singapore hosts 8 of the top 10 drug makers – now it needs commercial wins
content_en:
Industry insiders say the city state could serve as the gateway for Chinese medicines and a regional hub for rare-disease care.
Biochemists check a reactor used for manufacturing medical products at Takeda Pharmaceuticals in Singapore. Photo: AFP
Singapore has long sought to become Southeast Asia’s premier biomedicine hub – with its investments and initiatives having already attracted some of the world’s biggest pharmaceutical manufacturers.
But as competition for investment in the sector intensifies, industry experts say the city state needs to use its scientific strengths to produce commercially successful medicines, while overcoming the limitations of its small domestic market.
Bayer, the German pharmaceutical giant, hopes Singapore will become one of the first places to approve asundexian, its new blood thinner for preventing recurrent strokes. China approved the medicine last month. Bayer said on November 9 that the United States had done so too.
Sebastian Guth, chief operating officer of Bayer’s pharmaceuticals division, expects Singapore’s approval to follow soon.
A vessel passes a facility run by German chemical and pharmaceutical giant Bayer in Leverkusen. Bayer is hoping Singapore will become one of the first markets to approve its new blood thinner. Photo: AFP
“Singapore has a dependable and predictable regulatory environment with an emphasis on speed,” he told This Week in Asia earlier this month. “Stroke today is a leading cause of death and a leading cause of disability in every country around the world, including Singapore.”
China has the largest overall stroke burden globally, according to the World Stroke Organisation. A study in The Lancet Neurology estimated that the country had more than 26 million people living with stroke in 2021.
Size still matters
Singapore attracted S$4.4 billion (US$3.5 billion) of investment in its biomedical sciences sector last year, Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong said in May.
Eight of the world’s 10 largest biopharmaceutical companies – including Pfizer, GSK and Roche – operate manufacturing facilities in the city state, according to its Economic Development Board, the government agency responsible for attracting foreign investment.
The latest to set up shop is British drug maker AstraZeneca, which plans to open a US$1.5 billion plant to manufacture targeted cancer treatments by 2029. The Economic Development Board called this a “strong show of confidence” in the city state’s manufacturing capabilities and talent.
A staff member arranges exhibits at the AstraZeneca booth at the China International Import Expo on November 7. The British drug maker is expected to open a US$1.5 billion plant in Singapore in 2029. Photo: Xinhua
Analysts say Singapore’s weaknesses are its small domestic market, which provides companies with fewer customers over which to spread costs, and limited track record of commercial success in the sector, potentially pushing firms to look elsewhere for greater economies of scale.
Yoshihiro Suwa, a Singapore-based senior partner who leads pharma and healthcare work at consultancy Roland Berger, called the country’s limited experience turning biotech research into profitable medicines its biggest challenge, adding that China, Japan and South Korea were ahead of it in this regard.
Suwa said Singapore was not necessarily seen as a commercial gateway to Southeast Asia for pharmaceuticals, because of its small size. He cited Thailand as an example of a more popular regional market in which to launch new medicines.
Hong Kong may soon become another competitor, as it seeks to advance its biomedical hub ambitions. City authorities announced a new drug regulator in June last year, to be established by the end of 2026, whose long term-goal is independently assessing and approving drugs and medical devices, without relying on approvals from overseas.
Why Singapore appeals
Competition in the sector is growing because pharmaceutical companies are increasingly looking to the Asia-Pacific as a source of innovation, licensing deals and partnerships.
The United States, which helped pioneer modern biomedical research, long dominated the field and Guth said “that continues to be the case, but today it is complemented with Asia”.
He said Singapore had five things a global biomedicine hub needed: world-class scientists and institutions, access to capital, reliable regulation, strong protection of intellectual property and a willingness to pay for innovation. “I think Singapore realised early that the biomedical industry is a crown jewel,” Guth said.
The city state’s government made biomedicine the fourth pillar of the economy in 2000 and has since spent billions of dollars on research and innovation. Last month, it also announced its largest bioeconomy funding initiative to date: S$118 million (US$92 million) to help local start-ups and translate research into commercial applications.
Singapore realised early that the biomedical industry is a crown jewelSebastian Guth, Bayer Pharmaceuticals
Suwa called Singapore’s advanced biomedical sciences infrastructure “particularly impressive”, citing research clusters such as the Tuas Biomedical Park manufacturing hub and Biopolis – a purpose-built R&D campus – for facilitating “close collaboration” among academia, pharmaceutical companies and healthcare institutions.
Not only that, but Shriharsha Sarkar, a partner at L.E.K. Consulting who advises biopharma, medtech, diagnostics and healthcare service clients across the Asia-Pacific, said Singapore’s regulators were so respected that their approval could help medicines win approval elsewhere.
Many Southeast Asian regulators used “reliance-based pathways” for medicines, he said, which allowed them to lean on another authority’s reviews and often required less local data.
“Southeast Asia is made up of a dozen different systems, so launching in Singapore first lets companies prove the product, then roll it out market by market,” he said.
The region is entering “a golden age of regulatory sharing” amid increasingly pressing issues such as ageing populations and carer burnout, according to Simon Rosof, head of Asia-Pacific for Bayer’s pharmaceuticals division.
“There’s a lot more sharing of review processes and information ... regulatory authorities leveraging each other’s approvals to get therapies to patients more quickly,” he said.
[embedded media]
Bayer has its regional headquarters in Singapore’s central business district and works with local research institutions. In 2023, its investment arm joined other backers in launching 65Lab, a Singapore-based incubator that helps turn research from institutions such as National University of Singapore and the government’s Agency for Science, Technology and Research (A*Star) into commercial companies.
Guth said the city state supported each stage of drug development, from research to clinical trials and regulatory review.
“When I think about leading ecosystems in the biotech industry, Singapore clearly comes to mind,” he added.
A Chinese launchpad?
Industry experts advocate a two-pronged strategy for Singapore to fend off growing competition and overcome its market size constraints: working with China and specialising.
China’s drug approvals are rising fast, mainly driven by domestically developed medicines. In September, it set five-year targets that included having at least five products with annual global sales surpassing US$1 billion by 2030.
Sarkar said Singapore could become the hub through which Chinese medicines reach Southeast Asia and beyond. Only a fraction of innovative medicines approved worldwide reached the region because of fragmented regulation and limited budgets, he said.
“This gap is an opportunity and Chinese-originated innovation is well placed to fill it … the question is not if, but when,” he said, adding that China was increasingly developing drugs at competitive prices. “Singapore can anchor this: it can host regional commercialisation and regulatory strategy.”
A member of staff works at a biotech company in China’s Yunnan province in September. China’s drug approvals are rising fast, mainly driven by domestically developed medicines. Photo: Xinhua
Suwa said Singapore could also become a regional hub for treating rare diseases and for personalised medicine, meaning treatments tailored to an individual patient’s genetics or condition. Neighbouring countries might struggle to offer such therapies, he said, because they typically needed advanced infrastructure and highly specialised doctors. Investments in this area would give Singapore a “much broader role” in the region, Suwa added.
When asked how Bayer compared Singapore with other Asia-Pacific markets, Guth said the company did not view it in isolation.
“Innovation happens in conjunction and across ecosystems,” he said. “I think about Singapore also in the context of the Asia-Pacific, and the first and best-in-class medicines [that] are being advanced here.”

title_en: How the battle to host UN high seas treaty tests China’s push for global leadership
content_en:
Sudden Belgium-Chile dual-city pitch will test Beijing’s diplomatic reach and Global South backing as January vote looms, analysts say.
Fishing boats set sail from Zhoushan, in east China’s Zhejiang province, in August. Photo: Xinhua
A rival joint bid by Belgium and Chile to host the secretariat for the landmark UN high seas treaty could present a fresh diplomatic test for Beijing ahead of the 2027 vote.
Observers say the surprise November 6 announcement of their merged bid to oversee the Agreement on Biodiversity Beyond National Jurisdiction (BBNJ) will complicate China’s efforts to secure its first major UN body headquarters.
The agreement, which took effect in January, is the first legally binding framework to protect marine life in international waters covering nearly two-thirds of the world’s oceans.
The Belgium-Chile alliance comes just two months before treaty signatories are set to gather in New York in January to choose a permanent home for the secretariat and finalise rules for putting the pact into practice.
Under their dual-city model, Chile’s Valparaiso would house the secretariat’s core functions, while Brussels would host subsidiary body meetings and the treaty’s data-sharing infrastructure.
China, which has put forward the coastal city of Xiamen as a candidate, reacted furiously, accusing the two countries of “politicising the bidding process and dividing members into opposing camps”.
Beijing argues that a split or dual-city arrangement would undermine the secretariat’s operational efficiency and erode the interests of developing nations.
[embedded media]
Analysts say the diplomatic friction reflects how sharply the sudden partnership has shifted the contest.
Li Shuo, director of the Asia Society Policy Institute’s China Climate Hub, said the merged bids had made the hosting race “much tighter and more delicate”.
“Whether a proper resolution can be found will be a major test for all parties involved, as well as a test of China’s diplomatic skill and vision.”
Beijing actively pushed forward the treaty negotiations and signed the pact when it opened at the United Nations in 2023.
In October last year, China’s top legislature formally ratified the agreement, which aims to safeguard maritime areas beyond any nation’s jurisdiction and regulate access to marine genetic resources offering potential breakthroughs in pharmaceuticals.
Just before the treaty entered into force in January, China announced Xiamen would bid to host the new secretariat, marking the first time it has sought to house the headquarters of a multilateral environmental agreement.
Li said the joint bid would also be a test of how the world sees China’s growing willingness to lead.
“Now that China is willing to provide international public goods, how does China coordinate with the world to make this happen, and how does the world respond to China’s growing willingness?” he said.
“How the world responds will, in turn, tell how China approaches its future international leadership,” Li said. “If China is willing to do this, but gets shot down by the international community, it will affect China’s future appetite for leadership.”
Wang Jiangyu, a law professor at City University of Hong Kong, noted that while Beijing had a “very strong legal argument” against splitting the secretariat’s functions across two distant cities, likely to drive up participation costs and slow down decision-making, it faced a complex battle for support from the developing world.
He noted that both the Group of 77 – a coalition of 134 developing countries – and the 54-member African Group had welcomed China’s bid alongside the joint Chile-Belgium proposal.
“China is certainly one of the leaders – probably the biggest leader – of the Global South, but China cannot take this for granted,” Wang cautioned at a recent seminar hosted by the Huayang Centre for Maritime Cooperation and Ocean Governance, a government-backed think tank in southern China.
“We cannot take it for granted that we naturally represent the Global South.”
The Xiamen bid aligns with Beijing’s broader push in recent years to gain a greater voice in shaping global maritime rules. Its five-year plan to 2030, released in March, explicitly calls for China to proactively help formulate ocean governance rules and host “international maritime governance institutions”.
The apparently last-minute pact between Belgium and Chile – seen by some as an attempt to outmanoeuvre Beijing – has fuelled speculation that China could mount a pushback.
“I believe the Chinese government will also take corresponding actions to uphold the integrity and authority of the agreement, as well as China’s own legitimate rights and national dignity,” Wu Shicun, founding president of China’s National Institute for South China Sea Studies and chairman of the Huayang Centre, said at the same seminar.
[embedded media]
China has mounted a vigorous campaign – underscoring the symbolic weight of hosting the first major UN body in the Asia-Pacific, while arguing that basing the secretariat in Xiamen would amplify the voice of the Global South in global governance.
It has offered free office premises and accommodation, a US$3 million contribution to a trust fund for developing-country delegates, and a dedicated capacity-building fund – and pledged “efficient and free visa services” to boost “ease of travel” for officials, their families and delegates.
Some environmental advocates said in private that they were surprised by Beijing’s strong rhetoric against the joint Belgium-Chile bid, while others said China needed to promote its proposal more forcefully.
Dimitri de Boer, founding chief representative of environmental law charity ClientEarth’s China office, which has advised Beijing, pointed to the country’s recent strides in biodiversity protection backed by a series of new laws and policies.
He highlighted tougher rules against illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing, subsidy reforms to align with World Trade Organization rules, and steps to enforce the Port State Measures Agreement that China ratified in April 2025.
[embedded media]
At last month’s annual meeting of the Commission for the Conservation of Antarctic Marine Living Resources, Beijing put forward its first-ever proposal for a marine protected area. Some conservationists consider the move a breakthrough, given China’s track record of using its veto, alongside Russia, to block marine parks around the southern continent.
The Chinese government attached “great priority” to the BBNJ, de Boer said.
“I expect that if China had the secretariat, we would continue to see their best side on the ocean,” he added.
“That would really ensure continued political commitment from the very top in China – and in China, political commitment translates to real action.”
By Laura Zhou
